chapter_title: A Letter to God (including 'Dust of Snow' & 'Fire and Ice')

branches.theme: Prose Narrative: A Letter to God

details: Lencho's solitary house sits on the crest of a low hill overlooking the river and fields of ripe corn dotted with flowers.
Lencho anticipates a rich harvest requiring only a good downpour or gentle shower.
During dinner, rain starts falling; Lencho compares big drops to ten-cent pieces and small drops to five-cent pieces.
evidence_or_examples: Lencho's statement: 'These aren't raindrops falling from the sky, they are new coins.'

sub_branches.concept: The Hailstorm Crisis and Total Crop Ruin
details: Strong north-east winds bring large hailstones that fall for an hour across the valley, house, garden, hillside, and cornfield.
The entire field turns completely white as if covered with salt; not a leaf remains on trees, and corn is totally destroyed.
Lencho laments that even a plague of locusts would have left more than the hail.
evidence_or_examples: Lencho standing in the middle of the ruined field saying, 'A plague of locusts would have left more than this.'

sub_branches.concept: Lencho's Unshakable Faith and Letter to God
details: Despite facing starvation, Lencho retains absolute trust in divine providence.
On Sunday morning, he writes a letter addressed 'To God', requesting 100 pesos to sow his land again and live until the next harvest.
evidence_or_examples: Writing on the envelope: 'To God', dropped into the mailbox at the town post office.

sub_branches.concept: Post Office Staff Reaction and Benevolent Intervention
details: A postman sees the unique address and shows it to the postmaster.
The postmaster, an amiable fat man, initially laughs but quickly admires Lencho's profound faith.
To keep Lencho's faith intact, the postmaster collects contributions from staff, friends, and donates part of his own salary, gathering 70 pesos.
He puts the money in an envelope addressed to Lencho, signed simply 'God'.
evidence_or_examples: Postmaster collecting 70 pesos as an 'act of charity'.

details: Lencho receives the letter the following Sunday; he shows no surprise upon seeing money, but grows angry when counting only 70 pesos.
Convinced God could not miscalculate or deny his request, he immediately writes a second letter.
He requests God to send the remaining 30 pesos directly, advising against using the post office because the workers are 'a bunch of crooks'.
evidence_or_examples: Second letter excerpt: 'Send me the rest... But don't send it to me through the mail because the post office employees are a bunch of crooks.'

branches.theme: Poetic Study: Dust of Snow by Robert Frost

details: Frost chooses a crow and a poisonous hemlock tree—symbols associated with gloom and death—rather than traditionally beautiful nature elements.
A crow sitting on a hemlock branch shakes down a fine dust of snow onto the poet.
This small physical event instantly alters the poet's mood, saving the remainder of a regretful day from sorrow.
evidence_or_examples: Lines: 'Has given my heart / A change of mood / And saved some part / Of a day I had rued.'

branches.theme: Poetic Study: Fire and Ice by Robert Frost

details: Fire metaphorically represents burning human desire, lust, greed, and unbridled passion.
Ice metaphorically represents cold apathy, insensitivity, hatred, and rigid indifference.
Frost synthesizes that while fire (desire) is a rapid destroyer, ice (hate) is equally powerful and sufficient to end the world.
evidence_or_examples: Lines: 'From what I've tasted of desire / I hold with those who favour fire... I think I know enough of hate / To say that for destruction ice / Is also great.'
